content: Support mechanisms such as home-based distribution of HIV self-testing (HIVST) kits, training on HIVST, and in-person demonstrations or supervision should be carefully evaluated for their added benefits relative to the resources they require. These resource-intensive approaches may hinder scalability and should be implemented only for a limited duration. Over time, as HIVST programs mature, public awareness grows, and individuals gain experience with self-testing, the need for such intensive support is expected to decrease. Digital platforms, social media, and video or messaging tools can also be utilized to support self-testers. These methods are particularly appealing to younger populations and are generally less expensive than in-person support. It is essential to empower and actively involve communities in the development and adaptation of HIVST delivery and support models. Community members and individuals from key populations should meaningfully participate in the design and delivery of services. Community organizations, local non-governmental organizations, networks of people living with HIV, and representatives from key populations should be engaged in programming and HIVST delivery. Programs that are community-led and have strong community buy-in are more likely to succeed and achieve their objectives. Community engagement should also include educational efforts to raise awareness and minimize misuse or harm associated with HIVST. As with any HIV testing service (HTS), linking individuals to appropriate services after HIVST is critical to maximize its benefits. Those who test HIV-negative but remain at ongoing risk should be connected to prevention services. Individuals with reactive HIVST results should be supported in accessing confirmatory testing by trained providers using the national testing algorithm. If diagnosed as HIV-positive, they should be promptly initiated on antiretroviral therapy (ART). Where resources permit, strategies such as home-based ART initiation, in-person referral or peer navigation, and provider incentives can be considered to enhance linkage to care. When comparing the cost of HIVST to other HTS approaches, it is important to account for the full cost of service delivery, not just the cost of the HIVST kits. Delivery models in the private sector, such as pharmacy sales, may impose additional costs on users, which should be considered in the context of accessible and affordable HTS. Low-cost, high-impact HIVST models that prioritize key populations in strategic geographic areas are more likely to be cost-effective. Ongoing monitoring and evaluation (M&E) are necessary to optimize HIVST implementation. This requires developing an M&E plan, selecting key program indicators, collecting relevant data, regularly reviewing progress, and adjusting service delivery as needed. Pragmatic approaches, such as triangulating program data, ART coverage data, and special survey results, are essential for effectively monitoring HIVST outcomes and impact. Programs should explore the potential for integrating HIVST with other self-sampling technologies for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) such as chlamydia, gonorrhea, and human papillomavirus (HPV), as well as broader self-care interventions like contraception. This integration can support the delivery of comprehensive sexual and reproductive health services. HIV partner services, which involve offering voluntary HTS to the sexual and/or drug-injecting partners of people with HIV, are an effective way to identify additional individuals living with HIV. Partners diagnosed with HIV can be linked to treatment services, while those who are HIV-negative but at ongoing risk can be connected to effective prevention measures. Voluntary provider-assisted referral (also known as assisted partner notification) should be offered to people with HIV as part of a comprehensive package of testing and care. This approach has been shown to increase HTS uptake, identify additional undiagnosed HIV infections, and improve linkage to care among partners. HIV testing services for couples and partners, with support for mutual disclosure, should be offered to individuals with known HIV status and their partners. In all settings, biological children of parents with HIV should be routinely offered HTS. If found to have HIV or to be at high risk of infection through breastfeeding, they should be linked to treatment or prevention services within a broader package of voluntary provider-assisted referral. Social network-based HIV testing offers a complementary approach to reach the sexual or drug-injecting partners and social contacts of key population members. This method can expand the scope of testing to include HIV-negative partners and social contacts, making testing services more acceptable and normalizing their use. Social network-based approaches are particularly useful for reaching key populations and addressing confidentiality concerns. These approaches can improve the acceptability of partner services and reach individuals who might not otherwise test for HIV. The World Health Organization (WHO) conducted a systematic review to develop new guidance on social network-based HIV testing approaches. Evidence suggests that these approaches may result in higher HIV positivity rates compared to standard HTS or venue-based testing, indicating their potential for identifying additional HIV infections. Social network-based testing also tends to reach more first-time testers than standard HTS, although evidence on its effect on testing uptake remains inconclusive.
